title: Champagne Understood
subtitle: The true history behind champagne's most famous stories, from a monk who fought the bubbles to the long fight over a name.

episodes.title: The Monk Who Fought the Bubbles
episodes.hook: It is one of the loveliest stories in wine, that a monk tasted the first champagne and called out to his brothers about stars. The real Dom Pérignon was just as remarkable, though for quite different reasons.
cards: Dom Pierre Pérignon was a Benedictine monk from Sainte-Menehould, in Champagne. Only his baptism record survives, dated January 1639, so his exact birthday is not known.
In 1668 he was sent to the abbey of Hautvillers, on the hillside above the Marne near Épernay, and he remained there for the rest of his life.
His post was procureur, the abbey's steward, and with it came care of the vineyards, the cellars and the wine. Accounts rank the role second only to the abbot's.
He held that post until his death in 1715, so nearly half a century of harvests passed through his hands.
In his day, Champagne's reputation rested on still wine, and a wine that fizzed in the bottle was generally thought of as a fault rather than a delight.
The bubbles arrived uninvited. Cold winters could pause a fermentation, and when spring warmed the cellars the wine could stir again, sometimes bursting the fragile bottles of the time.
Historians describe much of the monk's effort as going into keeping his wine still, which gives the later legend a gentle irony.
His real gifts lay elsewhere. He worked to make clear white wine from black grapes, above all Pinot Noir, whose juice runs pale if it is kept away from the skins.
Accounts say he would not let the grapes be trodden, and that he used several presses so the colour in the skins had as little time as possible to reach the juice.
That care lives on in every blanc de noirs, a white champagne made only from black grapes, and in the gentle pressing for which Champagne is still known.
He is remembered for blending too. Historians are careful here: he did not introduce blending to Champagne, but he blended grapes from different vineyards before they went to the press.
In Champagne, blending is called assemblage, the art of combining grapes or wines from different places so that the whole is finer and steadier than any single part.
Drawing on several vineyards meant a poor season in one place could be balanced by another, a principle the great houses still rely on when they build a non-vintage blend.
So how did he come to be called the inventor of champagne? The story seems to begin in 1821, more than a century after his death, with a letter.
Its author was Dom Grossard, a later monk of the same abbey, who credited his predecessor with finding the secret of making wine sparkle.
Historians read the letter cautiously, partly because Grossard had reasons to burnish his abbey's name, and no earlier document is known to call Pérignon an inventor.
In 1889, for the Exposition Universelle in Paris, the champagne merchants' own association published a pamphlet presenting the monk as the creator of sparkling champagne.
The famous line, come quickly, I am tasting the stars, first appears in print advertising, which most sources date to the late nineteenth century, long after the monk's death.
In 1936 Moët & Chandon put on sale a prestige champagne bearing his name, and the legend and the label have travelled together ever since.
It is easy to see why the story stuck, because it is a beautiful one. The truth asks only that we admire him for patience and care rather than for one moment of discovery.
episodes.setup: If the monk was trying to keep the bubbles out, who first wrote down how to put them in? The answer takes us across the Channel, to London.

episodes.title: An English Argument
episodes.hook: If a monk did not invent sparkling champagne, then someone must have been the first to write down how to make wine sparkle. One strong candidate is an English physician, speaking to a learned society in London in 1662.
episodes.callback: We met Dom Pérignon, a careful steward of still wine whose legend was written long after him.
cards: Christopher Merret was an English physician and naturalist, and among the founding members of the Royal Society, the scientific society that met in London.
On 17 December 1662 he presented a paper to the Society with a wonderfully plain title: Some Observations concerning the Ordering of Wines.
In it he noted that the wine-coopers of his day added large quantities of sugar and molasses to their wines to make them drink brisk and sparkling.
That is the heart of a second fermentation. Sugar is added to a finished wine, the bottle is sealed, and yeast turns the sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide, which stays dissolved under pressure.
In Champagne today, the sugar and yeast added for this purpose are called the liqueur de tirage, and the second fermentation in the bottle is the prise de mousse, the capturing of the foam.
Merret's paper is often described as the earliest surviving written account of deliberately adding sugar to make a wine sparkle, which is why England's claim is taken seriously.
He presented it six years before Dom Pérignon arrived at Hautvillers in 1668, a date that makes the old story of a single French invention hard to keep.
Merret was describing a practice already in use among London's wine-coopers, rather than announcing an invention of his own.
A sparkling wine needs more than a recipe, though. It needs a bottle strong enough to hold the pressure, and in the seventeenth century that was the harder problem.
Here England had a stroke of fortune. An order of 1615 restricted the burning of wood in glass furnaces, to save timber for shipbuilding, so English glassmakers turned to coal.
Coal burned hotter than wood, and the coal-fired furnaces produced thick, dark glass that was considerably stronger than the bottles commonly used in France at the time.
English bottles were also given a raised ring of glass around the neck, so that a stopper could be tied firmly down and the gas kept inside.
The stopper mattered as well. The English used cork, imported from Portugal, which sealed far better than the wooden plugs and grease-soaked cloth then used in France.
Several names are put forward for the stronger bottle, Sir Kenelm Digby's among them, but writers disagree about who deserves the credit, so we leave it with the glassmakers in general.
Taken together, a written method, strong glass and a good cork all existed in England in the seventeenth century, which is why some historians say the English invented the bubbles.
That does not make Merret the inventor of champagne. The full method, with its clear wine and carefully removed sediment, was refined in Champagne itself in the years that followed.
Nor is England the only claimant. In Limoux, in the Languedoc in southern France, the sparkling Blanquette has its own story, set in the abbey of Saint-Hilaire.
The date usually given is 1531, said to come from the monks' papers. The oldest dated document that writers describe, an accounts ledger mentioning bottles of Blanquette, is from 1544.
Exactly how those early Limoux wines were made, and how lively they were, is hard to establish from the sources we could find, so Limoux's claim remains an open and intriguing one.
The honest picture is one of many hands: sugar and cork in London, a southern abbey's long tradition, and patient cellar work in Champagne, each adding something to the glass we know.
episodes.setup: Once champagne could keep its sparkle, it still had to please the people drinking it, and for a long time that meant a great deal of sugar.

episodes.title: When Champagne Was Sweet
episodes.hook: Most champagne today is dry, so it can come as a surprise that for much of the nineteenth century it was sweet, sometimes very sweet indeed. The story of how it became drier is also a story about Britain.
episodes.callback: We saw how a paper of 1662, English glass and good cork helped the bubbles survive the bottle.
cards: After the second fermentation, a champagne has almost no sugar left. Its final sweetness comes from the dosage, a small addition made just before the final cork goes in.
That addition is a blend of wine and sugar called the liqueur d'expédition, and the amount of sugar it brings decides whether the label says brut, demi-sec or doux.
Today a brut champagne has less than 12 grams of sugar per litre, while a doux, the sweetest style you will see on a label, has more than 50.
In the nineteenth century, sweetness was a matter of national taste, and houses adjusted the dosage of their wines for the different markets they shipped to.
Russian buyers were known for liking champagne very sweet. A style described as goût russe, Russian taste, is recorded at roughly 270 to 330 grams of sugar per litre.
Letters from Madame Clicquot's house to its agent in St Petersburg, studied by scientists in recent years, mention a dosage of nearly 300 grams per litre for Russian customers.
That is more than twenty times the upper limit for a brut today, which gives some sense of how differently those wines must have tasted.
Bottles of champagne recovered from a shipwreck in the Baltic Sea were analysed by scientists, who reported in 2015 that they held about 140 to 150 grams of sugar per litre.
The researchers suggested that this was too little sugar for Russian taste, and that the wine may have been bound for customers in the German lands instead.
British taste ran drier. The goût anglais, English taste, is recorded at roughly 22 to 66 grams per litre, which is still sweeter than any brut you might buy today.
London became the market where a much drier champagne first found a welcome, and two houses in particular are remembered for answering that wish.
Perrier-Jouët, an Épernay house, decided not to sweeten its 1846 vintage before sending it to London, a choice its own history ties to British connoisseurs' liking for a drier taste.
The house describes that wine as an early, lightly dosed champagne in the style we now call brut, and it still keeps bottles from that time in its cellars.
Pommery, in Reims, is often credited with the first champagne sold as brut, made from the 1874 vintage under Louise Pommery, a widow who ran the house.
That wine was made for the British market, where it is said to have fetched remarkable prices in London, and it helped make dry champagne fashionable there.
So which came first? Both houses have a fair claim, depending on what you count: an unsweetened shipment of the 1846 vintage, or a wine named and sold as brut from the 1874.
Either way, the direction was clear. Through the later nineteenth century and beyond, champagne grew steadily drier, with British taste leading the way.
The sweeter styles never vanished, and you can still find them today as demi-sec and doux, which can be lovely with fruit puddings and pastries.
One small curiosity survives on the label. A wine called extra dry is in fact a little sweeter than brut, a reminder that the words for dryness were coined in sweeter times.
So when you choose a brut today, you are enjoying a taste that took shape largely for British drinkers, long after champagne had first been made sweet.
episodes.setup: Sweet or dry, those early wines shared another problem, a cloud of spent yeast in every bottle. Next we meet the widow whose cellar found a way to clear it.

episodes.title: The Widow and the Riddling Table
episodes.hook: Sparkling champagne was once cloudy, because the spent yeast of its second fermentation stayed in the bottle. The way cellars learned to clear it is tied to a remarkable widow in Reims, and to the people who worked beside her.
episodes.callback: We followed champagne as it grew drier for British drinkers in the later nineteenth century.
cards: Barbe-Nicole Ponsardin was born in Reims on 16 December 1777, and she married François Clicquot, whose family ran a wine business in the city.
François died in 1805, and she took the business in hand at the age of twenty-seven. Widow in French is veuve, which is how her title came to be on the label.
The house still carries that name, Veuve Clicquot, and she guided it for decades, until her death in 1866 at the age of eighty-eight.
Her early years in charge were turbulent. In 1814, as Napoleon's wars were ending, her house sent more than ten thousand bottles by sea toward the Russian market.
Sources differ on the port where that cargo landed, Königsberg or St Petersburg, and on its exact size, though all of them put it above ten thousand bottles.
Her cellars are where the best-known answer to the cloudy bottle was developed. As the second fermentation ends, the spent yeast settles into a fine deposit called the lees.
Left in contact with the wine, the lees slowly give it flavour, a process called autolysis, but a cloudy glass was not what drinkers hoped to see when the cork came out.
The answer was remuage, or riddling. Bottles are tilted neck-down and turned a little at a time, so the deposit slides gently down the glass and gathers in the neck.
The tool for this is the pupitre, a wooden frame pierced with angled holes, which holds the bottles so their angle can be steepened little by little.
Most accounts date its development to around 1816 and credit Madame Clicquot together with her cellar master, Antoine Müller. The sources we found do not say how they shared the work.
A charming story says they began by cutting holes into a kitchen table. It is told as tradition, and we found no document to confirm it, so it is best enjoyed gently.
The design was refined by others later in the century, and many cellars now use machines called gyropalettes, which do in days what riddling by hand does over weeks.
Once the deposit sits in the neck, it is removed by dégorgement, or disgorgement: the neck is frozen, the bottle is opened, and the pressure pushes out the plug of sediment.
Her house is also linked with vintage champagne, a wine made only from the grapes of a single year and labelled with that year.
It is often called the first known vintage champagne, though sources differ on the year, some saying 1810 and others 1811.
The 1811 wine became known as the vintage of the comet, after the bright comet seen that year. People once believed comets brought great harvests, though there is no accepted reason they should.
She is also credited with rosé made by blending, that is, by adding a little still red wine to white. Her house and most accounts date this to 1818.
That word blending matters. Pink champagne was not new: Ruinart has found a record from 1764 of a pale pink wine, which was probably coloured another way, perhaps with elderberry.
So it is fairest to call her a pioneer of blended rosé, rather than the inventor of pink champagne itself.
Firsts are slippery things in Champagne's history, but her influence is not in doubt. Her name, and the riddling her cellar made famous, are part of champagne every day.
episodes.setup: The nineteenth century ended with champagne famous across the world, and then brought real hardship to the people who grew it.

episodes.title: Hard Years
episodes.hook: By the late nineteenth century champagne was famous and prosperous. Then came a tiny insect, a run of poor harvests and a bitter quarrel over fraud, which together brought years that the region still remembers.
episodes.callback: We stood in Madame Clicquot's cellars, where riddling helped make champagne clear.
cards: Phylloxera is a tiny, aphid-like insect from North America that feeds on the roots of vines. European vines have little defence against it, and infested vineyards slowly decline and die.
It had already spread through many French vineyards before it was found in Champagne, at Tréloup in the Aisne department, in August 1890.
It reached the Marne department two years later, in 1892, with outbreaks reported at Mardeuil and at Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, and from there it moved through the vineyards.
Its spread was slow at first and then much faster, and accounts describe it reaching the Montagne de Reims around the turn of the century.
Growers first relied on sulphur-based treatments of the soil, but the lasting answer, as elsewhere in France, was grafting.
Grafting means joining a European vine, such as Pinot Noir or Chardonnay, onto the roots of an American vine species whose roots can tolerate the insect.
The grapes still belong entirely to the European variety, because the fruit grows on the part of the plant above the graft. Only the roots are American.
Champagne's growers moved to grafted vines over the years that followed, with the region's agricultural services trialling American rootstocks in the later 1890s.
Replanting a whole vineyard was slow and costly, and a young vine takes several years to give a useful crop, so the burden fell heavily on the growers.
Phylloxera was not the only trouble. Mildew and frost struck in these years as well, and the harvest of 1910 was a disaster for many growers.
At the same time, some merchants were buying grapes and wine from outside the region and selling the result as champagne, which undercut the prices local growers could get.
Champagne had been given a legal boundary in 1908 that took in vineyards in the Marne and the Aisne. The Aube, to the south, was left outside it.
So in 1911 two grievances met. Growers in the Marne wanted the fraud stopped, while growers in the Aube wanted to be included within the Champagne name.
In January 1911, at Damery and Hautvillers, growers stopped vehicles carrying grapes and wine from outside the region and tipped their loads into the Marne.
In April, after a move in the Senate seemed to threaten the boundary, the unrest became far more violent, and the town of Aÿ was the worst hit.
The government sent troops to restore order. Accounts of how many soldiers were sent differ so widely that we have not repeated any figure here.
The Aube was soon given a place as a second zone, and in 1927 the boundary was settled so that it lay fully within Champagne.
The riots are often described as one of the pressures behind France's appellation system, which ties the name of a wine to the place where it is grown.
Out of these years came a region more closely defined and more closely protected, growing on new roots, and keenly aware of what its name was worth.
episodes.setup: Only three years after the riots, a far greater conflict reached Champagne, and its chalk cellars became shelters.

episodes.title: Champagne at War
episodes.hook: Champagne lies east of Paris, and in the twentieth century war came to its vineyards twice. The way people sheltered, worked and quietly resisted in the chalk beneath Reims is one of the most moving parts of its story.
episodes.callback: We saw phylloxera, failed harvests and the riots of 1911 test Champagne's growers.
cards: In August 1914, three years after the riots, Europe went to war. Within weeks the German army had swept through Champagne, and Reims came under occupation in early September.
After the Battle of the Marne the Germans were pushed back from Reims and Épernay, but not far, and the front line settled just outside Reims.
On 19 September 1914, German shells set fire to scaffolding around Reims Cathedral, where the kings of France were once crowned, and the fire did grave damage to the building.
The bombardment of Reims continued, with pauses, through most of the war. A chronicle of it published in 1917 already covered three full years.
Beneath the city lie the crayères, old chalk quarries that the champagne houses had taken over as cellars. They became a refuge for the people of Reims.
Underground there were schools, chapels, sleeping quarters and offices, and the houses carried on their work in the cellars as best they could.
In the Taittinger cellars, for example, a school was set up and named after General Augustin Dubail.
Above ground, the 1914 harvest had to be gathered all the same. With the men called up, the picking fell to the elderly, to women and to children.
Picking began on 21 September, with the front line only a short way off, and the pickers worked under the threat of shellfire and snipers.
Accounts of that harvest say that children were among those killed before the last grapes that could be reached were picked in October.
The 1914 wines were few, and some grapes were picked early for fear of a renewed attack, yet many writers remember the vintage for its remarkable longevity.
By the end of the war much of Reims, including its industrial buildings, had been destroyed, and the houses had a great deal to rebuild.
In 1940 war came again. France signed an armistice with Germany on 22 June, and Champagne lay in the zone the German army occupied.
The occupiers appointed an official to oversee the champagne trade, Otto Klaebisch, a man from the wine business who became known as the weinführer, the wine leader.
Sources describe him as a brother-in-law of Joachim von Ribbentrop, Hitler's foreign minister, though they differ about which wine firm he had come from.
His demands were heavy. Accounts say he could call for as many as 400,000 bottles a week, often for very little payment.
Houses and growers answered with quiet resistance. Stories are told of the best bottles being hidden behind false walls in the chalk, though such tales are hard to document.
In 1941 the trade created the Comité Interprofessionnel du Vin de Champagne, the CIVC, a body that brought growers and houses together and that still exists today.
Robert-Jean de Vogüé, of Moët & Chandon, represented the houses within it, and he dealt with Klaebisch on their behalf.
In November 1943 he was arrested in Klaebisch's office and sentenced to death. The sentence was commuted, he was sent to camps in Germany, and he survived the war.
Days after his arrest, the CIVC's secretary called the region's workers out on strike, an open protest made under occupation.
Klaebisch left in the summer of 1944, and Champagne came out of both wars with a deep conviction that its cellars, and its name, were worth defending.
episodes.setup: Having protected their cellars, the people of Champagne turned to protecting something less tangible, the name on the bottle.

episodes.title: The Fight for the Name
episodes.hook: Champagne is the name of a place, and the people who grow it have spent more than a century asking the world to keep it that way. The effort has reached treaties, courtrooms, a Spanish restaurant and a Swiss village.
episodes.callback: We went beneath Reims through two world wars, and met the man who bargained for its cellars.
cards: To the people of Champagne, the word is not a style of wine but a place: only sparkling wine from that region, made under its rules, may carry the name.
By the nineteenth century, though, champagne had become a common word for sparkling wine in many countries, and producers far from the region used it freely.
An international agreement signed in Madrid in 1891 dealt with false indications of where goods came from, and it is often cited as an early basis for protecting the name.
After the First World War, the Treaty of Versailles of 1919 went further. Its Article 275 bound Germany to respect the wine and spirit appellations protected by the Allied countries.
That article is often linked to a dispute between France and Germany over sparkling wines and brandies sold under French names, and it curbed the use of the word among the treaty's parties.
The United States signed the treaty but never ratified it, which is one reason American sparkling wines could go on calling themselves champagne for so long.
In 2006 the United States and the European Community agreed that new American wines would not use the name, though brands already approved before then could keep it.
That is why you may still see the word on a few long-established American labels, a use that lawyers describe as grandfathered.
Within the European Union, Champagne is a protected designation of origin, or PDO, a legal status that reserves the name for wine from the defined region made under its rules.
The protection reaches beyond wine. In 2021 the EU's Court of Justice ruled that it can also cover services, in a case about a Spanish restaurant business called Champanillo.
Champanillo means little champagne. The court left the final decision to the Spanish courts, but explained that a name can be barred if it calls the protected wine to mind.
Spain has its own long history with the word. Many Spanish speakers still say champán or champaña in everyday speech, but under EU law Spanish sparkling wine may no longer be marketed as champagne.
In England, in 1960, champagne producers won a case against a company selling Spanish Champagne, and the judge held that the label was likely to mislead buyers.
Spain's own great sparkling wine took the name Cava, meaning cellar, and sources place the adoption of that name at various points between 1959 and the early 1970s.
Perhaps the most poignant case is a village in the Swiss canton of Vaud that is itself called Champagne, and that has vineyards of its own.
Under an agreement between Switzerland and the European Union, the village's wine could no longer carry the village's own name after 2004.
Its growers have challenged the rule since, but in 2021 a court in Vaud confirmed that the name is protected for the French region alone.
Russia took a different path. A law signed on 2 July 2021 reserved shampanskoye, the Russian word for champagne, for sparkling wine made in Russia.
Under that law, imported champagne had to be described as sparkling wine on its back label, which upset the champagne trade a great deal.
Moët Hennessy briefly paused its shipments to Russia, then within days agreed to comply, a sign of how much the market and the name both mattered.
It can seem a great deal of effort for one word. To the growers, though, the name carries their soil, their rules and their history, which is why they guard it so carefully.
episodes.setup: We end, as every thread here does, with an honest scorecard of what held up, what has changed, and what we chose to leave out.

episodes.title: Scorecard
episodes.hook: Every thread here ends with an honest account. This is where we gather what has held up, what has been overtaken, the popular versions we have gently corrected, and what we chose to leave out, with our reasons.
episodes.callback: We followed the name of Champagne through treaties, courtrooms and a Swiss village that shares it.
cards: First, what has held. Dom Pérignon was a real and gifted monk, steward of the abbey of Hautvillers from 1668 until his death in 1715.
His care in pressing black grapes to make white wine, and his blending of grapes from different vineyards, are the parts of his legend that historians still accept.
Christopher Merret's paper of December 1662 remains one of the earliest known written descriptions of adding sugar to wine to make it sparkle.
Madame Clicquot's cellar is still the one most often credited with riddling, around 1816, and her house with an early vintage champagne and an early blended rosé.
Next, what has been overtaken. Champagne has travelled a long way from the goût russe, and a brut today has less than 12 grams of sugar per litre.
Grafting onto American roots, once an emergency remedy, is now simply the ordinary way vines are grown in Champagne.
Riddling by hand has given way in many cellars to machines called gyropalettes, though some houses still riddle certain wines by hand.
And the Aube, left outside Champagne's first boundary in 1908, has been fully part of the region since 1927.
Some popular versions deserve a gentle correction. Dom Pérignon did not invent champagne, and there is no evidence that he spoke of tasting the stars; that line comes from later advertising.
The idea of Pérignon as inventor seems to begin with Dom Grossard's letter of 1821 and a trade pamphlet of 1889, both written long after his death.
The English did not invent champagne either, but they wrote down the sugar method early, and they had the strong glass and cork to keep the bubbles in.
And Madame Clicquot did not invent pink champagne. A pink wine appears in Ruinart's records in 1764; her contribution was rosé made by blending.
Finally, what we left out, and why. We have not named a single year for the first vintage champagne, because sources divide between 1810 and 1811.
We have given no firm date for Limoux's sparkling wine. The 1531 date is widely repeated, but the oldest dated record that writers describe is from 1544.
We have not said who first made champagne dry, because Perrier-Jouët and Pommery each have a different and reasonable claim, depending on what you count.
We left out Sir Kenelm Digby's part in the strong English bottle, because writers disagree about how much of it was his.
We also left out the number of soldiers sent in 1911 and the total number of bottles taken during the occupation, because the accounts differ too widely.
And we have not retold the kitchen-table story as fact, or said how Madame Clicquot and Antoine Müller shared the work, because no record we found settles it.
Thank you for reading this far. We hope that the next time a cork is drawn, the stories in the glass feel a little truer, and every bit as lovely.
